reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: An inherited arrhythmia syndrome in which adrenergic stress provokes ventricular arrhythmias in a structurally normal heart
Typically presents in childhood or adolescence with exercise- or emotion-induced syncope, seizures, or sudden cardiac death
The resting ECG and echocardiogram are characteristically normal, which can lead to misdiagnosis as epilepsy or vasovagal syncope
Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, with beat-to-beat alternation of the QRS axis, is a hallmark, though polymorphic VT is also seen
Exercise or catecholamine provocation testing reproducibly elicits the arrhythmia and is central to diagnosis
Most cases arise from mutations affecting cardiac calcium handling, notably the ryanodine receptor and calsequestrin
Beta-blockade forms the cornerstone of therapy, with flecainide and sympathetic denervation as adjuncts and defibrillators reserved for selected patients
Family screening and genetic testing are important because the first manifestation may be sudden death
reference.pathophysiology: CPVT results from abnormal handling of calcium within cardiomyocytes. Mutations, most commonly in the ryanodine receptor gene, cause excessive diastolic leak of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during adrenergic stimulation. The resulting calcium overload generates delayed afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, which under sympathetic drive produce bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Because the myocardium is structurally normal, the arrhythmia is functional and strongly dependent on catecholamine exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Epilepsy or other neurological causes of collapse
additionalInvestigations: Exercise stress testing to reproduce ventricular arrhythmias
Ambulatory ECG monitoring during exertion or emotional stress
Catecholamine (isoproterenol) provocation when exercise testing is not feasible
Resting ECG and echocardiography to confirm a structurally normal heart
Genetic testing for ryanodine receptor and related mutations
redFlags: Syncope or cardiac arrest during exertion or emotional stress
Bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on testing
Family history of exercise-related sudden death or unexplained drowning
reference.prognosis: Untreated CPVT carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death, often before adulthood. With consistent beta-blocker therapy, additional antiarrhythmic drugs, and lifestyle modification, arrhythmic events fall substantially, and prognosis improves markedly, though breakthrough events can still occur and warrant device or surgical intervention.
pitfalls: Attributing exertional collapse to epilepsy or simple faints and missing the diagnosis
Being falsely reassured by a normal resting ECG and echocardiogram
Failing to perform provocative testing when clinical suspicion is high
Incomplete beta-blockade or poor adherence leaving patients unprotected
Neglecting to screen and counsel relatives
management: Non-selective beta-blockade, particularly nadolol, as first-line therapy against catecholamine-triggered ventricular arrhythmia
Add flecainide to suppress residual calcium-driven ectopy when beta-blockade alone is inadequate
Lifestyle modification with avoidance of strenuous exercise and emotionally stressful triggers
Left cardiac sympathetic denervation for arrhythmia refractory to drug therapy
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for high-risk patients such as aborted cardiac arrest or breakthrough events on treatment
Serial exercise stress testing and Holter monitoring to verify arrhythmia suppression
Cascade genetic and clinical screening of first-degree relatives for ryanodine receptor and calsequestrin variants
Emergency response plan with automated external defibrillator availability and family resuscitation training
